analytic.title: Hierarchical Scheduling of Periodic Messages in Open System

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper describes a hierarchical scheme for scheduling periodic messages of distributed r eal-time applications in a cluster of PCs connected by a Myrinet. The scheme allows the developer of each real-time application to validate the schedulability of the application as if it were running alone on slower dedicated processors and network. A simple acceptance test is provided. According to the test, the operating system can determine whether to admit a new real-time system application into a system without having to perform detailed global schedulability analysis. Simulation results show that the hierarchical scheduling scheme outperforms the corresponding one-level heuristic algorithms. An o p en system prototype on a Myrinet cluster PCs running Windows NT uses this hierarchical scheme.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The dramatic performance increase in computing systems and high-speed local area networks, together with the development of new low latency and high bandwidth communications paradigms e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4 , has led to an increasing desire to run high performance real-time applications e.g., high-speed data acquisition, real-time simulation, and decision support on a cluster of PCs connected by a high performance network. The advantages of a PC cluster over a high performance machine include lower cost and higher availability. This fact has motivated us to design an open distributed, real-time environment on a PC cluster. In an open environment, we can decide whether an application can meet its timing requirements based on a few overall parameters e.g., its required processor and network bandwidth, rather than requiring a global schedulability analysis. The operating system starts an application to run in the real-time mode when requested by the application, if the application passes a simple acceptance test. Once the application is allowed to run in real-time mode, the operating system provides e ective timing isolation to guarantee the application's end-to-end schedulability regardless of the behavior of other applications in the system. In contrast, in a closed system, we can determine the schedulability of each application only by global schedulability analysis based on timing attributes and resource usages of all applications that may run simultaneously. The need for detailed timing information and the high cost of global schedulability analysis severely limits the congurability of such a system and keeps the system closed despite its comformity to standards. Systems based on traditional approaches to real-time scheduling are closed in this sense.

In addition to providing an overview of our open distributed real-time environment, this paper describes a two-level scheme for scheduling network tra c over a Myrinet 2 . This scheme extends the uniprocessor open system environment, which was developed recently by Deng,et al. 6,7 , to a PC cluster. The uniprocessor open system e ectively provides a slower virtual processor for each of the real-time applications sharing a physical processor. Similarly, the two-level network scheduling scheme creates a virtual slower network for each application running on the PC cluster. The capacity of the virtual network required by an application is decided by the application developer based on a timing analysis which assumes that the application runs alone on a cluster of slower PCs connected by a slower network.

The two-level scheme guarantees that if the real-time messages of any application are schedulable on a slower network of the required capacity and the open system admits the application, they will be schedulable in the distributed open environment.

Our two-level scheme uses the Weighted-Round-Robin WRR scheme 10 at the lower level to partition the network among applications. The WRR scheme was developed for scheduling real-time messages through packet switches; other well known algorithms for this purpose include the Weighted Fair Queueing WFQ 8, 9 , Framed-Round-Robin FRR 11 , and Stop-and-Go S&G 12 algorithms. Unlike packet switches, which provide bu er spaces, Myrinet switch is bu erless. Our scheme partitions time on all input and output links into identical xed size time slots and synchronizes time slots across all the links. A con ict is said to occur during a time slot if the packets arriving on two or more input links in the time slot are destined for the same output link. Past work on scheduling periodic messages through a bu erless switch 13, 1 4 , 1 5 have focused on assigning packets to time slots to minimize schedule length and maximize link utilization. Our two-level scheme uses several of these algorithms at the high level to schedule messages in individual applications. The main objective of our two-level scheme is to provide timing guarantee and isolation to real-time applications, but we will show later that the scheme also yields better link utilization than the corresponding onelevel algorithms.

Following this introduction, Section 2 describes our open system model and states our assumptions. It also brie y describes Myrinet, as well as Fast Messages 1, 2 , which is the low level messaging mechanism our open system uses to transfer data. Section 3 describes the two-level scheduling scheme used by the operating system to schedule messages from multiple applications while creating an illusion to each application that there is a dedicated network for the application. Section 4 presents a simulation study of the two-level scheduling algorithm. Section 5 describes our design of the distributed open system on a Myrinet running Windows NT and our current implementation e ort. Section 6 summarizes the paper.

div.head: System Model and Assumptions
div.p: Figure 1 shows our model of a distributed open system. Multiple distributed applications run on a cluster of PCs or workstations. We denote real-time applications by A k for k = 1; 2; :::; N. The number N of real-time applications may v ary during runtime as some applications terminate and new ones start.

div.head: Workload and Scheduling Hierarchy
div.p: To validate that a real-time application A k can meet its timing requirements, its developer analyzes its schedulability based on the assumption that the application runs alone on dedicated processors and network whose speed and bandwidth are fractions of that of the physical processors and network. The minimum fractional processor speed k and fractional network bandwidth B k at which an application A k is schedulable can be thought o f a s t h e required p r ocessor capacity and network capacity of the application. In other words, k and B k are the processor speed and network bandwidth, respectively, required by A k normalized with respect to the physical processor speed and link bandwidth.

We focus here solely on periodic message streams, which we will refer to simply as message streams or streams. The basic unit of transmission is a packet; packets are transmitted nonpreemptively. The two-level scheduling scheme described in the next section partitions time into time slots of length equal to the time required to transmit a packet at the physical link bandwidth. We assume that the period p k;i of every message stream i from every application A k is an integer multiple of the length of time slots, and the rst period of the stream begins at the beginning of some time slot. Each instance of stream i from A k takes c k;i time slots to transmit over the physical link, and its relative deadline is p k;i . In our discussion, we call the stream by the tuple src k;i , dst k;i , c k;i , p k;i or dst k;i , c k;i , p k;i when we w ant to make its source src k;i and destination dst k;i or only its destination explicit. The utilization of the stream is u i = c k;i =p k;i . The utilization Ul of link l is the sum of utilizations of all the message streams that traverse link l. At initiation time, all applications run in the nonreal-time mode. The operating system serves non-real-time applications on the best e ort basis. When a distributed real-time application requests admission into the open system i.e. to execute in real-time mode, it speci es in its request its required network capacity a s well as its required processor speed. The system accepts the application if after granting the request, the utilization of every link is less than or equal to one and the application passes the acceptance test of every participating processor.

Each task in the application consists of a chain of CPU jobs and message transmission jobs. On each processor, a two-level CPU scheduling scheme makes it possible for the operating system to guarantee the timing constraints of CPU jobs of individual applications while allowing the CPU jobs of each application to be scheduled according to the algorithm chosen for the application. Details on how the CPU scheduling scheme works can be found in 6, 7 . When a job requests networking services, it passes its CPU execution budget 1 to a communication server in the system. The CPU time consumed by the communication server to send and receive messages on behalf of the job is thus charged to the application to which the job belongs. The communication server schedules all outgoing and incoming messages and guarantees the timely delivery of each message, while at the same time provides timing isolation to all other real-time applications in the system. We will describe the design of communication server in more detail in Section 5.

The algorithm used to schedule out-bound message streams is also a two-level scheme. The message streams from every application are scheduled by a high level scheduler HLS. Speci cally, the high-level scheduler HLS 0 schedules message streams from all non-real-time applications in the system on FIFO basis. This is how messages are scheduled in general purpose operating systems. The high-level scheduler HLS k k 1 for a real-time application A k schedules message streams from the application using the algorithm chosen by the developer of the application. At each processor, each high level scheduler HLS k has a ready queue to hold out-bound message streams of application A k , while the actual sending and receiving of data is controlled by a low level scheduler LLS. We will describe the scheduling algorithm used by the schedulers in Section 3. 1 The execution budget in our model is analogous to Mercer's reserve abstraction 16 . Mercer's reserve abstraction serves the purpose of accurately accounting for any activity which i n vokes user-level service o ered by the operating system. The budget replenishment s c heme is used to control the resource e.g. CPU usage of a job and is allocated based on the requesting application's reserved capacity a s w ell as the execution time or message length and deadline of a job.

div.head: Myrinet and FM
div.p: Our prototype implementation uses Myrinet 2 and the send and receive mechanism provided by Illinois Fast Messages 1 . Myrinet is a 4-or 8-port gigabit-persecond bu erless switch. The core of the switch is a pipelined crossbar. Whenever the header of a packet reaches the switch, the remaining portion of the packet is forwarded to the desired output link as soon as the header is decoded, if the output link is not being used for the transmission of another packet. Otherwise, if the output link is in use, the packet is said to be blocked. When a packet is blocked at the switch, a simple STOP GO ow control mechanism blocks the source of that packet from sending more packets.

The network interface has a programmable processor, called LANai. The interface has 1024K SRAM for storing the Myrinet Control Program MCP and for packet bu ering. It also contains three DMA engines for transfering data between host memory and LANai memory and between LANai memory and the network. Illinois Fast Messages FM is a low-level messaging layer that bypasses the operating system to provide direct access to Myrinet. FM achieves 92MB s bandwidth and less than 10 s latency by mapping the LANai memory directly into the host address space. It coordinates between the host and LANai so messages can be transferred under DMA control from LANai queues into corresponding host queues to minimize the need for data copying during message transfer.

Wormhole routing is often used for scheduling packet transmissions through bu erless switches because of its simplicity and performance. However, it can induce blocking. If a packet is blocked for more than 50ms, the Myrinet ow control protocol assumes deadlock and the packet is dropped. In order to avoid dropped packets, our network scheduling scheme constructs a con ict-free schedule. Moreover, the CPU jobs that process incoming data are scheduled in the open system so as to ensure that the receiving bu er never over ows. Thus the system avoids unbounded blocking as well as link reset. Finally, Myrinet provides in-order packet delivery. This allows us to treat Myrinet as a reliable network. In summary, our approach to providing end-to-end guarantees depends on the communication server's ability t o s c hedule for timely completion of sending and receiving CPU jobs, to control the interaction between each CPU and the corresponding LANai card, and to construct a global con ict-free schedule which predictably multiplexes periodic message streams on network links.

div.head: Network Scheduling Scheme
div.p: Again, the goal of our network scheduling scheme is to create a virtual environment for each real-time application by reserving a fraction of the network capacity for the application. Applications run together without compromising the real-time performance of each other and without requiring schedulability analysis be done on a per-message basis across applications. respectively. For the sake of simplicity, the tuples listed in the tables do not contain the names of the sources; the source of each message stream is given by the label of the row containing the tuple name of the stream. Again, the relative deadline of every message is equal to Figure 4: Global Schedule its period. The required network capacity of each application is 0.5. There is no non-real-time application in the system.

The gures also show con ict-free feasible schedules of the message streams of the applications if each w ere to run alone on a dedicated system in which the network bandwidth is half of the physical network bandwidth. Hence, the amount of time in terms of the number of time slots on the physical network required to send each instance of a message stream i from application A k is twice the message length c k;i given by the tuple name of stream i in the table. For example, each instance of B 1;1 ; 3; 12 takes 6 slots of time to transmit over the virtual input link which has only half the physical bandwidth. In the gure, each time line labeled by a source processor name shows the time intervals during which message streams from the source are transmitted to the switch on the corresponding input link in the virtual slow network. For example, the rst time line in Fig-

ure 2 shows that message stream B 1;1 ; 3; 12 from A to B are transmitted on the virtual input link A from time 0 to 6, from 12 to 18, from 26 to 32, and so on. 2 The con ict-free schedule for each application is constructed by a high level scheduler of the application using the earliest deadline rst row-by-row algorithm, one of four heuristic scheduling algorithms which we will describe later in this section.

While the developer of a real-time application is free to choose any algorithm for the high level scheduler of the application, the low level scheduler LLS uses the weighted-round-robin algorithm to divide the physical network bandwidth among applications based on the applications' required capacities. In general, the round length used by LLS must be no greater than the minimum period of all message streams in the system. By using a su ciently small round length, the LLS ensures that there is at least one round in each period of every message stream. The acceptance test described later assumes that LLS adjusts the round length each time when it conducts the test and admits a new real-time application. Alteratively, the LLS may choose a xed round length, and thus, imposes a lower limit on the periods of all message streams supported by the system.

In our example, LLS gives each of applications A 1 and A 2 half the time slots in each round. The minimum period of all message streams in A 1 and A 2 is 12. We choose the round length to be 6. Hence, each application is allowed to send 3 packets in each round. The LLS transmits packets from HLS 1 's ready queue during slot 1 through 3 in each round, then switches to HLS 2 's ready queue in slots 4 through 6. Figure 4 shows a feasible con ict-free schedule of the applications running together on the physical network. We can see that all the message streams from the applications share the physical network without interfering each other, and no message misses its deadline.

div.head: High Level Scheduler
div.p: The high level scheduler HLS k of each real-time application A k uses one of four heuristic algorithms to schedule message streams from the application through the switch. They are Earliest Deadline First Row-by-Row EDF-RR, Minimum Laxity First Row-by-Row MLF-RR, Earliest Deadline First using System of Distinct Representatives EDF-SDR, and Minimum Laxity First using System of Distinct Representatives MLF-SDR algorithms. All the algorithms represent the trafc of the application by a tra c matrix T. The x; y-th element T x;y of the tra c matrix contains a descriptor of each message stream whose source is processor x and destination is processor y. The tables in Figure 2 and3 can be thought of as tra c matrices of the applications; each element has only one descriptor. The result is a con ict-free schedule of length equal to the LCM least common multiple of the periods of all message streams of the application.

The row-by-row algorithms schedules tra c speci ed by each row of the tra c matrix at a time. In other words, such an algorithm schedules the message stream from each source i.e., on each input link in turn, in order as the sources appear in the tra c matrix.

According to the EDF-RR algorithm, message streams from each source are scheduled on the EDF basis whenever possible. Speci cally, the high level scheduler schedules the message streams from the rst source listed in the tra c matrix on the EDF basis. This is the schedule of input link 1. After message streams from sources 1; 2; :::; x , 1 are scheduled, the scheduler then schedules message streams from source x given by the x-th row of the tra c matrix. It does so by c hoosing a packet to be transitted over the input link x in each time slot at a time, starting from the rst time slot. For each time slot, it chooses the packet which has the earliest deadline among all ready but not yet scheduled packets that are from source x and do not con ict with any o f the packets from sources 1; 2; :::; x , 1 scheduled to be transmitted in the time slot. Because of the possibility of con icts, the packet chosen for a time slot may not be one with the earliest deadline among all ready packets from x, and some time slots on input link x may be left idle despite some packets being ready. Consequently, the schedules of message streams on all input links except input link 1 may not be EDF schedules.

In our example in Figure 2, the schedule of input link source A i.e., the rst source listed in the table is an EDF schedule. The rst instance of message stream B 1;5 ; D 1;5 ; 4; 18 has an earlier deadline than the rst instance of B 1;4 ; C 1;4 ; 6; 36. We note that on a slower network half of the speed, the time to transmit each message instance is twice the length given by the table. Moreover, there is no con ict in slots 1-8.

Hence the rst instance of B 1;5 ; D 1;5 ; 4; 18 is scheduled in slots 1-8 on link B. During slots 9 and 10, only the rst instance of B 1;4 ; C 1;4 ; 6; 36 is ready, but it cannot be scheduled in the slots. The reason is that the rst instance of A 1;2 ; C 1;2 ; 2; 36 has already been scheduled during these slots on input link A and it is also to be routed to output link C, the same output link as B 1;4 ; C 1;4 ; 6; 36. Consequently, the rst instance of B 1;4 ; C 1;4 ; 6; 36 is scheduled in slots 10-22. The second instance of B 1;5 ; D 1;5 ; 4; 18 is released at slot 18.

However, it cannot be scheduled immediately after the rst instance of A 1;2 ; C 1;2 ; 2; 36 completes because of con ict with the rst instance of A 1;3 ; D 1;3 ; 5; 36 and is, therefore, scheduled in slots 28-36. It is easy to see that the schedule for input link B is not an EDF schedule. Neither are the schedules for input links C and D for the same reason.

The MLF-RR algorithm is same as the EDF-RR algorithm except the minimum laxity rule instead of the EDF rule is used. Laxity of a message instance at any time is equal to its deadline minus the current time and the time required to send the remaining packets in the message instance. When choosing a packet to be transmitted on input link x during each time slot, the high level scheduler chooses the packet with the minimum laxity among all ready packets from source x which d o not con ict with packets scheduled to be transmitted during the time slot on input links 1; 2; :::; x , 1.

In contrast to row-by-row algorithms, the SDR algorithms look at all message streams speci ed by the tra c matrix before making any scheduling decision. The EDF-SDR algorithm rst sort all message instances given by the tra c matrix according to their deadlines.

Let d 1 d 2 ::: d m be a list of distinct deadlines of all message instances that are to be transmitted during a hyperperiod i.e., an interval of length equal to the LCM of periods of all message streams of the real-time application A k under consideration. During each time slot, a high level scheduler using this algorithm schedules as many packets as possible with the deadline d 1 , then d 2 , and so on in order of increasing deadline d i , until i = m or the slots on all input links at and before d m are taken. The MLF-SDR algorithm is the same as EDF-SDR, except that at each time slot the packets of message instances with minimum laxity are chosen instead of those with the earliest deadline.

The application developer selects one of the four algorithms and validates the schedulability of the message streams of the application based on the assumption that the application runs alone in a slower virtual network and all messages are scheduled by a one-level scheduler using the selected heuristic algorithm. After the required processor and network capacities are determinded, the developer can initialize the real-time application and then ask the operating system to admit the application into the open system.

div.head: Acceptance Test
div.p: The open system subjects each new real-time application A k to an acceptance test. In addition to the set of parameters required for the acceptance test on each processor, the application also provides in its request its required network capacity, the message scheduling algorithm k , and the minimum period k of all its message streams. Figure 5 Input provided by the new application A k when A1; :::; A k,1 are in the system: the required network capacity U k ; the message scheduling algorithm k ; the minimum period k of all message streams in A k .

div.head: Algorithm:
div.p: 1. Conduct acceptance test in 6, 7 on the application to guarantee that the application is schedulable on each processor.
2. Calculate C = minjf j g; j = 1 ; :::; k.

3. Find the e ective required capacity U 0 j = dUj Ce=C, o f Aj for j = 1 ; :::; k. To explain the test, we recall that the LLS partitions the network on weighted-round-robin basis. Whenever a new real-time application A k starts to execute in the real-time mode, the LLS updates the round length to the minimum period of all message streams in the system. The required network capacity of the application is U k . However, because messages are preemptible only at the boundary of each slot, the operating system needs to round up the requested capacity based on the round length. This modi ed value is called the e ective required capacity in Figure 5. Speci cally, the round length and message length are speci ed in terms of number of time slots. Step 3 rounds up U k to avoid assigning a fraction of a time-slot. A k passes the network acceptance test if after granting the e ective required network capacity t o A k , the sum of the e ective required capacities of all real-time applications in the system does not exceed the total capacity of one.

After the application A k passes the acceptance test, the operating system in each of the participating nodes creates a high level scheduler HLS k . Again, HLS k uses the algorithm selected by the application developer and schedules the individual messages of application A k according to this algorithm. The lower level Myrinet scheduler updates its send schedule so that each application is given its reserved number of time slots in each round. The slots that are not assigned to real-time applications are used for non-real-time tra c, i.e. messages in HLS 0 's ready queue.

div.head: Simulations
div.p: We conducted a simulation study to evaluate the hierarchical scheduling scheme. For this purpose, we simulated two systems, a closed system and an open system. The systems consist of identical sets of real-time applications. We randomly generated message streams src i , dst i , c i , p i for each real-time application such that the input and output link utilization are less than or equal to the application's required capacity. We c hose the required capacities for the real-time applications in order to simulate three di erent scenarios: 1 network bandwidths are equally divided among multiple applications; 2 network bandwidths are divided among applications with a range of bandwidth requirement; 3 one application reserves a large fraction of the network bandwidth while the rest share the remaining bandwidth e.g. one application is ooding the network while the rest may be simple control programs that pass small packets between processors in the cluster.

The schedulability of both an open system and a closed system depend on the parameters of the system and the real-time applications running on the system. These parameters include the number of applications in the system, the number of message streams in each application, variation of message periods, scheduling algorithm, utilization of each link, and the overall system load distribution. To study how each of these param-eters a ects the overall schedulability, we conducted a number of experiments. In each experiment, we generated a set of synthetic workload by randomizing one particular parameter while keeping the others xed. Every real-time application in our study contains only periodic message streams.

For each experiment, we applied one of the heuristic algorithms described in Section 3 in an attempt to nd a con ict-free schedule of the message streams of all applications in a closed system. Since we cannot use di erent s c heduling algorithms for di erent applications in the closed system, we used the same scheduling algorithm for all real-time applications in the corresponding open system as well. Speci cally, w e s c heduled the message streams from each real-time application in the open system according to the same algorithm, assuming that the message streams are transmitted on a dedicated virtual slower network. The schedules of individual applications are merged as described in the previous section to generate an overall schedule of all applications in the open system. We then counted how often the algorithm found con ict-free feasible schedules. This count gives the relative success rate of each heuristic algorithm in both systems. The solid lines in Figure 6 and 7 give the performance for the four heuristic algorithms described above in closed systems. We generated 10000 sets of message streams to yield negligibly small con dence intervals. Periods are selected so the schedule length i.e. the least common multiplier of the periods of all message streams in each set does not exceed 420. We k eep the average link utilization at 90. The network is a 4-port Myrinet. We see that the SDR-based algorithms outperform the RR-based. MLF-based algorithms do a little better than the EDF-based algorithms. This is expected because MLF-based algorithms consider the number of packet remaining to be sent in addition to the deadline. Hence laxity is a better measure of urgency than deadline alone. SDR-based algorithms are more complex, but the performance gain justi es the complexity. We expected they would outperform the Row-by-Row based algorithms, because they take a global point of view before selecting the packet with earliest deadline or minimum laxity. The parameters that a ect the success rate in nding a con ict free schedule are switch dimensions, schedule length, and average utilization of all links. Philp 13 shows that the success rate drops rapidly as these three parameters increase.

For the simulation of an open system, we splitted the set of message streams used in the simulation of the corresponding closed system into two subset, each with link utilization up to 45, and considered them as from two applications. Two applications each asks for 50 of the total network capacity and each utilizes 90 of its requested bandwidth. We apply EDF-RR, MLF-RR, EDF-SDR, MLF-SDR to each set independently and then combine the two s c hedules together as described in the previous section. We discover that the success rate improves dramatically using the hierarchical scheduling scheme, as shown in Figures 6 and7. Even though we apply the same heuristic algorithms for high level scheduling as in the closed system, scheduling each set separately reduces the size of the scheduling problem and hence improves the success rate.

div.head: NumberofApplications and Load Distribution
div.p: We examine how the number of applications in the open system a ects the schedulability of the network. For this experiment, we simulated systems with two, three, four, and ve real-time applications. Table 1 lists their required capacities. Moreover, we allowed the load distribution of each system to vary. Table 1 lists the required capacities of the applications in each system. Again, the link utilization is 90 and the switch size is 4x4. Figure 8 shows the success rate in each system. The system that contains one application is a closed system. For system with two or more applications, the dark color bar is the success rate when the network capacity i s equally divided among the applications. The light gray bar shows the success rate when the required capacities of the applications are harmonic fractions of the total network capacity. We intend to simulate a spectrum of capacity requirements and harmonic value was chosen for the sake of simplicity. The shaded bar shows the success rate when one application dominates in the cluster while the rest of the applications only utilize a small fraction of the network bandwidth.

We see that the success rate increases as more applications are allowed to run in the system. This is to be expected since each HLS has a smaller number of messages and the heuristic algorithms perform better. Furthermore, we observe that the load distribution makes a di erence in the success rate as well. Among systems with the same number of applications, the success rate is highest when the network capacity is equally distributed among applications. For example, in a system running four real-time applications, the success rate of scheduling messages from applications each using 1 4 of the total bandwidth is substantially higher than that of one application requesting 3 4 of the bandwidth while the each of the other applications requests 1 20, especially for the simpler Row-by-Row based algorithms. This is a mixed e ect of schedule length and period variation.

In general, we observe that the hierarchical scheduling scheme allows a larger set of periodic message streams to be scheduled in the network compared to a closed system. It reduces the scheduling problem size and yields a higher system utilization.

div.head: Design and Implementation
div.p: We are currently implementing a prototype of the hierarchical scheduling scheme in a distributed environment which runs on a Myrinet cluster of PCs running Windows NT. A real-time application speci es its required network capacity, a s w ell as the bu er size for its send and receive queues. If the operating system accepts an application, it establishes a communication context

div.p: Figure 8: Success rates as the number of applications increases. N=4, U=90, L=420

for the application, generates a con ict free schedule, and then switches the application to run in the realtime mode. In essence, the communication context of an application is a partition of the LANai memory that is mapped directly into the application's address space.

The con ict-free schedule speci es which application is allowed to transmit in each time slot within a round. The Myrinet Control Program MCP running on each node loads the new schedule and resets the LANai card. After the application is switched to run in realtime mode, ready instances of its message streams are inserted into the send queue in the communication context according to the high level scheduling algorithm chosen by the application developer. Packets in the send queue of each HLS k are transferred in the order given by the application's schedule under DMA control out to the network when the low level scheduler schedules application A k to send.

div.head: Interaction between CPU and network scheduling
div.p: As discussed in section 2, in order to provide end-toend guarantee to applications, the interaction between CPU and network scheduling is crucial. The hierarchical network scheduling scheme guarantees that packet arrives at receiving host before its deadline. The prototype uses a user-level communication server to provide network services. To keep accurate accounting of the CPU resource, the communication server is executed by a passive server 7 .

A passive server is given only a very small amount o f processor bandwidth and uses its own execution budget solely for administrative purposes. The processor time the communication server uses to perform any service is charged to the application requesting the service.

A real-time client application requests a service by calling one of two real-time application programming interface RTAPI calls, SendData and RecvData. When an application A k calls the function SendData, it passes in the request the data to be sent and the handle to the server, as well as its own execution budget and deadline for consuming the budget. In response to the request, the communication server creates a new work thread in its own address space. The work thread inherits this budget and deadline. This thread is then inserted into the ready queue of the passive server on EDF basis. When the work thread is scheduled to run, it copies data into the communication context that has been reserved for the application. Also, it schedules the packets in the application's send queue according to the algorithm used by the application. Based on the required capacity the application speci ed and the length of each s c hedule cycle, each communication context receives credits to send at the beginning to each cycle. The LLS is implemented in the Myrinet Control Program. It sends U 0 k C packets every C time-slots from the message queue in application A k 's communication context, where C is the minimum period of all message streams in the system.

A client application calls RecvData to request the communication server to process incoming data on its behalf. Similar to SendData, the RecvData function also causes a transfer of CPU budget from the requesting application to the communication server. If the data to be received is not available when the requesting application calls RecvData, the call e ectively freezes the requesting application: the server of the requesting application has no budget, and the communication server holding the application's budget cannot execute on behalf of the application as the data is not available. To circumvent this problem, the application rst makes a call to WaitData to indicate it is expecting incoming data. If the data is available, WaitData returns imme-diately. Otherwise, the CPU thread calling WaitData is blocked. Since WaitData function does not transfer budget to the communication server, other threads in the requesting application may still execute during the time when the calling thread is blocked. When incoming data arrives, the communication server processes the message header and then noti es the receiving application about the source and length of the message. The application is expected to respond immediately. As soon as the thread calling RecvData is scheduled by the CPU scheduler and the application server is replenished, CPU budget is transferred from the application to the communication server to process the packets and copy the message from the communication context to the application's address space.

The communication server is an important component in providing end-to-end guarantees in our design. It is responsible for conducting the network acceptance test, implementing the hierarchical network scheduler, and controlling the interaction between CPU and the network. The two-level network scheduler guarantees that the message arrives at its receiving host before its deadline, and the CPU scheduler guarantees that the CPU thread that is to process the message is dispatched before its deadline. Each application has its own dedicated high level CPU and network schedulers and a separate communication context. The CPU budget replenishment s c heme and the low level Myrinet scheduler together guarantees the end-to-end timing properties of the distributed applications in the system. Also, each application has its own message bu ers in the communication context. An overload in an application and hence an over ow in one bu er may cause blocking and packet drops in the application alone but has no e ect on other real-time applications.

div.head: Implementation Issues
div.p: In our current implementation, there are several issues that require further study. Firstly, processors experience some clock drift. A s k ew between the di erent processors' execution of their schedules may cause network blockings. We make use of the feedback-based synchronization scheme proposed by Connelly and Chien 3 . However, the self-synchronizing schedule used in the feedback-based synchronization takes up several slots periodically to execute, e.g., in a 8-node cluster, the synchronization scheme takes 8 slots every 200 slots. We need to account this nonpreemptable section in our schedulability analysis. Secondly, the current scheme gives little support for non-real-time application. Unlike the total bandwidth server used for CPU scheduling 6, 7 , once a schedule is constructed, the slots reserved for real-time applications are left empty if the application has no packet to send. These slots cannot be used e ectively for best e ort tra c because the non-real-time tra c from one processor may block the realtime tra c from other processors in the cluster. Thirdly, for multi-switch networks, the complexity t o construct global con ict-free schedules grows exponentially with the number of switches. We need good heuristic schemes for scheduling periodic hard real-time message streams through multi-switch Myrinet; we are currently working on this problem.

div.head: Summary
div.p: This paper proposes an environment a n d a s c heduling scheme for independently developed distributed realtime applications on Myrinet. The open system architecture relies on two-level hierarchical schemes for both processor and network scheduling. On a processor, a CPU scheduler and a network scheduler are created for each real-time application. The CPU scheduler schedules the real-time threads, and the network scheduler schedules the messages from the application. The real-time application developer chooses a scheduling algorithm for each o f the schedulers when requesting for admission to run in the open system. All nonreal-time applications are scheduled together by a timeshared scheduler on each CPU and on the FIFO basis on the network. A communication server, which is implemented as a real-time application in the system, controls the low level Myrinet scheduler to schedule all the high level network schedulers on each processor. The open system has a simple acceptance tests for both processors and the network. The test makes it possible to start an arbitrary real-time application at run-time without having to know the detailed timing attributes of the requesting application and to conduct a costly global schedulability analysis. The proposed hierarchical scheduling scheme allows higher network utilization as well as providing isolation among real-time applications. A misbehaved application cannot e ect the schedulability o f other applications running concurrently in the system.
